claim: The transactional outbox pattern addresses how to update the database and send a message atomically.
quote: How to atomically update the database and send messages to a message broker?
notes: Chris Richardson, microservices.io. Forces section adds: '2PC is not an option.'

claim: Outbox solution: write the message to the database in the same transaction as the business change; a separate process sends it to the broker.
quote: The solution is for the service that sends the message to first store the message in the database as part of the transaction that updates the business entities. A separate process then sends the messages to the message broker.

claim: The outbox message relay can publish a message more than once (crash after publishing, before recording), so consumers must be idempotent.
quote: Message relay might publish a message more than once. It might, for example, crash after publishing a message but before recording the fact that it has done so. When it restarts, it will then publish the message again. As a result, a message consumer must be idempotent, perhaps by tracking the IDs of the messages that it has already processed.
notes: Text on page begins 'The Message relay might...' in a bullet; quoted from 'Message relay' onward.

claim: Polling publisher: the relay polls the outbox table; drawback: ordering is tricky.
quote: Publish messages by polling the database’s outbox table.
notes: Benefits: 'Works with any SQL database'. Drawbacks listed: 'Tricky to publish events in order', 'Not all NoSQL databases support this pattern'.

claim: Transaction log tailing: read the database's transaction log (MySQL binlog, Postgres WAL, DynamoDB streams) and publish outbox inserts.
quote: Tail the database transaction log and publish each message/event inserted into the outbox to the message broker.
notes: Mechanisms listed: 'MySQL binlog', 'Postgres WAL', 'AWS DynamoDB table streams'. Drawbacks include 'Requires database specific solutions' and 'Tricky to avoid duplicate publishing'.

claim: Idempotent consumer: insert the message id into a PROCESSED_MESSAGE table inside the same transaction; a duplicate fails the primary key and is discarded.
quote: After starting the database transaction, the message handler inserts the message’s ID into the PROCESSED_MESSAGE table. Since the (subscriberId, messageID) is the PROCESSED_MESSAGE table’s primary key the INSERT will fail if the message has been already processed successfully.

claim: A saga is a sequence of local transactions; on failure, compensating transactions undo prior steps; coordinated by choreography or orchestration.
quote: A saga is a sequence of local transactions. Each local transaction updates the database and publishes a message or event to trigger the next local transaction in the saga. If a local transaction fails because it violates a business rule then the saga executes a series of compensating transactions that undo the changes that were made by the preceding local transactions.

claim: Two ways to coordinate sagas: choreography (events) and orchestration (an orchestrator tells participants what to do).
quote: Choreography - each local transaction publishes domain events that trigger local transactions in other services Orchestration - an orchestrator (object) tells the participants what local transactions to execute
notes: Original is a bulleted list; hyphens are the page's own.

claim: Saga drawbacks: no automatic rollback, and no isolation between concurrent sagas.
quote: Lack of isolation (the “I” in ACID) - the lack of isolation means that there’s risk that the concurrent execution of multiple sagas and transactions can use data anomalies.
notes: Typo 'can use data anomalies' is on the page (sic). Other drawback: 'Lack of automatic rollback - a developer must design compensating transactions that explicitly undo changes made earlier in a saga rather than relying on the automatic rollback feature of ACID transactions'.

claim: SQS standard queues deliver at least once; duplicates and out-of-order delivery can happen; ordering is best effort.
quote: Standard queues ensure at-least-once message delivery, but due to the highly distributed architecture, more than one copy of a message might be delivered, and messages may occasionally arrive out of order. Despite this, standard queues make a best-effort attempt to maintain the order in which messages are sent.

claim: Standard queues suit any workload whose application tolerates duplicates or reordering.
quote: Standard message queues are suitable for various scenarios, as long as your application can handle messages that might arrive more than once or out of order.

claim: A received message stays in the queue but is hidden; if not deleted before the visibility timeout expires it becomes visible again. Default is 30 seconds.
quote: The visibility timeout starts as soon as a message is delivered to you. During this period, you're expected to process and delete the message. If you don't delete it before the timeout expires, the message becomes visible again in the queue and can be retrieved by another consumer. The default visibility timeout for a queue is 30 seconds, but you can adjust this to match the time your application needs to process and delete a message.

claim: Even within the visibility timeout, SQS does not guarantee a message will not be delivered twice.
quote: However, due to the at-least-once delivery model of Amazon SQS, there's no absolute guarantee that a message won't be delivered more than once during the visibility timeout period.

claim: Use ChangeMessageVisibility as a heartbeat to extend; the visibility timeout has a hard 12-hour maximum from first receipt.
quote: If your processing time varies or may exceed the initially set timeout, use the `ChangeMessageVisibility` action to extend the visibility timeout while processing the message. Keep in mind that the visibility timeout has a maximum limit of 12 hours from when the message is first received. Extending the timeout doesn't reset this 12-hour limit.

claim: Setting visibility timeout to 0 releases a message immediately for other consumers.
quote: If you decide not to process a received message, terminate its visibility timeout by setting the `VisibilityTimeout` to 0 seconds through the `ChangeMessageVisibility` action. This immediately makes the message available for other consumers to process.

claim: Crashed or failed consumers do not lose messages: the message reappears after the timeout.
quote: If you don't process and delete a message before the visibility timeout expires—due to application errors, crashes, or connectivity problems—the message becomes visible again in the queue. It can then be retrieved by the same or a different consumer for another processing attempt. This ensures that messages aren't lost even if the initial processing fails.
notes: Quote contains an em-dash in the AWS original; keep verbatim in citations but do not reuse in page prose.

claim: Standard queues allow about 120,000 in-flight messages; FIFO in-flight limits now depend on active message groups.
quote: For standard queues, there's a limit of approximately 120,000 in-flight messages, depending on queue traffic and message backlog. If you reach this limit, Amazon SQS returns an `OverLimit` error, indicating that no additional messages can be received until some in-flight messages are deleted. For FIFO queues, limits depend on active message groups.
notes: The visibility-timeout page no longer states the 20,000 FIFO figure; see sqs_inflight_limit_fifo.

claim: SQS keeps messages 4 days by default, 14 days at most.
quote: By default, a message is retained for 4 days. The minimum is 60 seconds (1 minute). The maximum is 1,209,600 seconds (14 days).

claim: Maximum SQS message size is now 1 MiB (raised from 256 KiB in 2025); larger payloads go via S3 with the Extended Client Library.
quote: The minimum message size is 1 byte (1 character). The maximum is 1,048,576 bytes (1 MiB).
notes: Correction to the common belief of 256 KB. Date of the change: see sqs_1mib_announcement.

claim: Visibility timeout default 30 s, min 0, max 12 hours.
quote: The default visibility timeout for a message is 30 seconds. The minimum is 0 seconds. The maximum is 12 hours.

claim: Message delay (timer) max is 15 minutes.
quote: The default (minimum) delay for a message is 0 seconds. The maximum is 15 minutes.

claim: FIFO queues (non-high-throughput) handle 300 transactions per second per action per partition, or 3,000 messages per second with batches of 10.
quote: Each partition in a FIFO queue is limited to 300 transactions per second, per API action (`SendMessage`, `ReceiveMessage`, and `DeleteMessage`). This limit applies specifically to non-high throughput mode. By switching to high throughput mode, you can surpass this default limit.

claim: With batching, non-high-throughput FIFO reaches 3,000 messages per second.
quote: If you use batching, non-high throughput FIFO queues support up to 3,000 messages per second, per API action (`SendMessage`, `ReceiveMessage`, and `DeleteMessage`). The 3,000 messages per second represent 300 API calls, each with a batch of 10 messages.

claim: High-throughput FIFO: up to 70,000 TPS (700,000 messages per second batched) in the largest regions; lower elsewhere (2,400 TPS default).
quote: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), and Europe (Ireland): Up to 70,000 transactions per second (TPS).
notes: Batched: 'Up to 700,000 messages per second (10x the non-batch limit of 70,000 TPS).' All other regions: 'Default throughput of 2,400 TPS.'

claim: maxReceiveCount in the redrive policy is how many receives before a message moves to the dead-letter queue.
quote: Use a **redrive policy** to specify the `maxReceiveCount`. The `maxReceiveCount` is the number of times a consumer can receive a message from a source queue before it is moved to a dead-letter queue. For example, if the `maxReceiveCount` is set to a low value such as 1, one failure to receive a message would cause the message to move to the dead-letter queue.

claim: Messages can be moved back out of a DLQ (redrive) after the bug is fixed.
quote: Move messages out of the dead-letter queue using [dead-letter queue redrive](sqs-configure-dead-letter-queue.md).

claim: A DLQ on a FIFO queue breaks strict ordering.
quote: Don't use a dead-letter queue with a FIFO queue if you don't want to break the exact order of messages or operations.

claim: Set the DLQ retention longer than the source queue's, because standard-queue expiry uses the original enqueue time.
quote: Thus, it is a best practice to always set the retention period of a dead-letter queue to be longer than the retention period of the original queue.

claim: FIFO queues preserve order strictly and support many ordered message groups in one queue.
quote: The order in which messages are sent and received is strictly preserved and a message is delivered once and remains unavailable until a consumer processes and deletes it.
notes: Same page: 'Additionally, FIFO queues support *message groups* that allow multiple ordered message groups within a single queue. There is no quota to the number of message groups within a FIFO queue.'

claim: Within a message group, the next message is not delivered until the in-flight one is deleted or its visibility timeout expires.
quote: For FIFO queues, messages with the same message group ID are processed in a strict sequence. When a message with a message group ID is in-flight, subsequent messages in that group are not made available until the in-flight message is either deleted or the visibility timeout expires.

claim: FIFO deduplication: a retried SendMessage within the 5-minute deduplication interval does not create a duplicate; dedup ID is explicit or a SHA-256 of the body.
quote: Unlike standard queues, FIFO queues don't introduce duplicate messages. FIFO queues help you avoid sending duplicates to a queue. If you retry the `SendMessage` action within the 5-minute deduplication interval, Amazon SQS doesn't introduce any duplicates into the queue.
notes: Content-based option: 'This instructs Amazon SQS to use a SHA-256 hash to generate the message deduplication ID using the body of the message'. 'Exactly-once processing' here is producer-side dedup within 5 minutes, not end-to-end exactly once: a consumer that crashes before DeleteMessage still sees the message again.

claim: FIFO in-flight limit is now 120,000 (not the older 20,000 figure).
quote: FIFO queues support a maximum of 120,000 in-flight messages (messages received by a consumer but not yet deleted). If this limit is reached, Amazon SQS does not return an error, but processing may be impacted.
notes: Correction: the commonly cited 20,000 FIFO in-flight limit is outdated per current AWS quota page.

claim: Long polling waits up to 20 seconds for a message, cutting empty responses and cost.
quote: When the wait time for the `ReceiveMessage` API action is greater than 0, *long polling* is in effect. The maximum long polling wait time is 20 seconds. Long polling helps reduce the cost of using Amazon SQS by reducing the number of empty responses (when there are no messages available for a `ReceiveMessage` request) and false empty responses (when messages are available but aren't included in a response).
notes: Markdown link around ReceiveMessage removed.

claim: AWS raised the SQS maximum payload from 256 KiB to 1 MiB in August 2025.
quote: Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) has increased the maximum message payload size from 256 KiB to 1 MiB

claim: RabbitMQ automatic ack treats a message as delivered once sent: higher throughput, less safety (effectively at-most-once if the consumer crashes).
quote: In automatic acknowledgement mode, a message is considered to be successfully delivered immediately after it is sent. This mode trades off higher throughput (as long as the consumers can keep up) for reduced safety of delivery and consumer processing. This mode is often referred to as "fire-and-forget".
notes: Same page: 'automatic message acknowledgement should be considered unsafe and not suitable for all workloads.' The at-most-once label is our gloss, not RabbitMQ wording.

claim: Unacked deliveries are requeued when a consumer's channel closes; consumers must be idempotent; redeliveries carry redeliver=true.
quote: Due to this behavior, consumers must be prepared to handle redeliveries and otherwise be implemented with idempotence in mind. Redeliveries will have a special boolean property, redeliver, set to true by RabbitMQ. For first time deliveries it will be set to false.
notes: Link and code formatting stripped. 'this behavior' refers to automatic requeueing of unacknowledged deliveries when a channel or connection closes.

claim: basic.qos prefetch count caps unacknowledged deliveries per channel; RabbitMQ pauses delivery at the cap.
quote: This is done by setting a "prefetch count" value using the basic.qos method. The value defines the max number of unacknowledged deliveries that are permitted on a channel. When the number reaches the configured count, RabbitMQ will stop delivering more messages on the channel until at least one of the outstanding ones is acknowledged.

claim: Quorum queues detect poison messages that keep getting requeued.
quote: Quorum queue support handling of poison messages, that is, messages that cause a consumer to repeatedly requeue a delivery (possibly due to a consumer failure) such that the message is never consumed completely and positively acknowledged so that it can be marked for deletion by RabbitMQ.

claim: Since RabbitMQ 4.0 quorum queues have a default delivery limit of 20; beyond it the message is dropped or dead-lettered.
quote: Starting with RabbitMQ 4.0, the delivery limit for quorum queues defaults to 20.
notes: Same page: 'When a message has been redelivered more times than the limit the message will be dropped (removed) or dead-lettered (if a DLX is configured).' Implication: without a DLX, poison messages are silently dropped after 20 tries.

claim: RabbitMQ Streams are an append-only log that consumers can read repeatedly (non-destructive), unlike classic queues.
quote: Streams model an append-only log of messages that can be repeatedly read until they expire.
notes: Also: 'one or more consumers subscribe to it and read the same messages as many times as they want.'

claim: PostgreSQL docs: SKIP LOCKED gives an inconsistent view, so it is not for general work, but suits multiple consumers on a queue-like table.
quote: With SKIP LOCKED, any selected rows that cannot be immediately locked are skipped. Skipping locked rows provides an inconsistent view of the data, so this is not suitable for general purpose work, but can be used to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table.
notes: Section 'The Locking Clause'. SKIP LOCKED available since PostgreSQL 9.5.

claim: NOTIFY sends an event to LISTENing clients, and inside a transaction it is delivered only if the transaction commits.
quote: Firstly, if a NOTIFY is executed inside a transaction, the notify events are not delivered until and unless the transaction is committed.
notes: Opening line: 'The NOTIFY command sends a notification event together with an optional "payload" string to each client application that has previously executed LISTEN channel for the specified channel name in the current database.'

claim: River (Go) stores jobs in the same Postgres as app data; enqueueing in the same transaction means the job exists if and only if the data change commits.
quote: Being built for Postgres, River encourages the use of the same database for application data and job queue. By enqueueing jobs transactionally along with other database changes, whole classes of distributed systems problems are avoided. Jobs are guaranteed to be enqueued if their transaction commits, are removed if their transaction rolls back, and aren't visible for work _until_ commit.
notes: README on master branch (fetched 2026-10-04), not a pinned tag. Longer treatment: https://riverqueue.com/docs/transactional-enqueueing which says 'When you enqueue a job in River, you can do so in a transaction with any other changes you're making such as inserting a user record or adding a corresponding profile record.'

claim: Oban (Elixir) enqueues jobs atomically with other database changes; backed by PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite3.
quote: **Transactional Control** — Enqueue a job along with other database changes, ensuring that everything is committed or rolled back atomically.
notes: Contains an em-dash in the original. Tagline: 'Robust job processing in Elixir, backed by modern PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite3.' main branch, not pinned.

claim: Solid Queue is the default Active Job backend in new Rails 8 apps and uses FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
quote: Solid Queue can be used with SQL databases such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQLite, and it leverages the `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` clause, if available, to avoid blocking and waiting on locks when polling jobs.
notes: Same README: 'Solid Queue is configured by default in new Rails 8 applications.'

claim: Graphile Worker (Node.js) stores jobs in Postgres; jobs are never lost and run at least once, usually exactly once, with exponential-backoff retries.
quote: As you would expect from a job queue, Graphile Worker ensures that your jobs will not get lost (thanks to Postgres' transactional guarantees), and that each job will execute at least once. Most jobs will execute exactly once; but if something goes wrong (either with the job itself, with worker, or with your infrastructure) then Graphile Worker will automatically retry the job at a later time, following exponential backoff.
notes: Same text on https://worker.graphile.org/docs

claim: Procrastinate (Python) uses PostgreSQL to store tasks, manage locks and dispatch.
quote: Procrastinate is an open-source Python 3.10+ distributed task processing library, leveraging PostgreSQL 13+ to store task definitions, manage locks and dispatch tasks.

claim: PGMQ is an SQS-like message queue implemented as a Postgres extension, with visibility timeouts and archiving.
quote: A lightweight message queue. Like [AWS SQS](https://aws.amazon.com/sqs/) and [RSMQ](https://github.com/smrchy/rsmq) but on Postgres.
notes: Repository moved from tembo-io/pgmq to the pgmq org. Its README also claims 'Guaranteed "exactly once" delivery of messages to a consumer within a visibility timeout', which is a vendor claim scoped to one visibility window; across timeouts it is at-least-once like SQS.

claim: Celery acks a task just before running it by default (so a started task is never rerun); tasks should ideally be idempotent; acks_late is for idempotent tasks.
quote:
Ideally task functions should be :term:`idempotent`: meaning
the function won't cause unintended effects even if called
multiple times with the same arguments.
Since the worker cannot detect if your tasks are idempotent, the default
behavior is to acknowledge the message in advance, just before it's executed,
so that a task invocation that already started is never executed again.
notes: Rendered: https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html. RST markup kept verbatim. Default Celery is therefore at-most-once per started execution; acks_late makes it at-least-once.

claim: task_acks_late (default off) acknowledges after the task runs, not right before.
quote:
Default: Disabled.

Late ack means the task messages will be acknowledged **after** the task
has been executed, not *right before* (the default behavior).

claim: With acks_late a task may run multiple times if the worker crashes mid-execution.
quote:
Note: This means the task may be executed multiple times should the worker
    crash in the middle of execution.  Make sure your tasks are
    :term:`idempotent`.

claim: Celery FAQ: retry handles expected Python errors (the task is still acked); acks_late handles worker crashes; combine both only if the task is idempotent.
quote:
So use retry for Python errors, and if your task is idempotent
combine that with `acks_late` if that level of reliability
is required.
notes: Earlier in the same answer: '`Task.retry` is used to retry tasks, notably for expected errors that is catch-able with the :keyword:`try` block. The AMQP transaction isn't used for these errors: **if the task raises an exception it's still acknowledged!**' Rendered at https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/faq.html#faq-acks-late-vs-retry

claim: Even with acks_late, Celery acks a task if the worker process is killed, unless task_reject_on_worker_lost is set, which can cause message loops.
quote:
Even if :setting:`task_acks_late` is enabled, the worker will
acknowledge tasks when the worker process executing them abruptly
exits or is signaled (e.g., :sig:`KILL`/:sig:`INT`, etc).

Setting this to true allows the message to be re-queued instead,
so that the task will execute again by the same worker, or another
worker.
notes: Followed by warning: 'Enabling this can cause message loops; make sure you know what you're doing.'

claim: worker_prefetch_multiplier defaults to 4 messages per process, which can distribute long tasks unfairly.
quote:
Default: 4.

How many messages to prefetch at a time multiplied by the number of
concurrent processes. The default is 4 (four messages for each
process).

claim: With the Redis broker, an unacked task is redelivered after the visibility timeout, default 1 hour.
quote:
The visibility timeout defines the number of seconds to wait
for the worker to acknowledge the task before the message is redelivered
to another worker.
notes: Same page: 'The default visibility timeout for Redis is 1 hour.'

claim: ETA/countdown/retry tasks scheduled further out than the Redis visibility timeout get redelivered and executed again, in a loop.
quote:
If a task isn't acknowledged within the :ref:`redis-visibility_timeout`
the task will be redelivered to another worker and executed.

This causes problems with ETA/countdown/retry tasks where the
time to execute exceeds the visibility timeout; in fact if that
happens it will be executed again, and again in a loop.
notes: Also: 'Broker is not a database, so if you are in need of scheduling tasks for a more distant future, database-backed periodic task might be a better choice.'

claim: Run only one Celery beat scheduler per schedule, or tasks are duplicated.
quote:
You have to ensure only a single scheduler is running for a schedule
at a time, otherwise you'd end up with duplicate tasks.

claim: RQ (Redis Queue) keeps every failed job with its exception in the FailedJobRegistry.
quote:
The default safety net for RQ is the `FailedJobRegistry`. Every job that doesn't
execute successfully is stored here, along with its exception information (type,
value, traceback).
published: rq 2.12.0 is latest on PyPI; doc fetched from master
notes: Rendered: https://python-rq.org/docs/exceptions/

claim: RQ retries are opt-in per enqueue with Retry(max, interval), interval may be a list for growing delays.
quote:
# Retry up to 3 times, with 60 seconds interval in between executions
queue.enqueue(my_func, retry=Retry(max=3, interval=60))

# Retry up to 3 times, with longer interval in between retries
queue.enqueue(my_func, retry=Retry(max=3, interval=[10, 30, 60]))
notes: Code sample from the docs.

claim: Arq is a job queue for asyncio Python backed by Redis.
quote: Job queues and RPC in python with asyncio and redis.
published: arq 0.28.0 latest on PyPI; docs from main
notes: Rendered: https://arq-docs.helpmanual.io/

claim: Arq deliberately prefers running a job more than once over zero times, so jobs must be idempotent.
quote: **Jobs may be called more than once!**
notes: Continues: 'All *arq* jobs should therefore be designed to cope with being called repeatedly if they're cancelled, eg. use database transactions, idempotency keys or redis to mark when an API request or similar has succeeded to avoid making it twice.' and '**In summary:** sometimes *exactly once* can be hard or impossible, *arq* favours multiple times over zero times.'

claim: Arq custom job IDs prevent the same job being enqueued twice until it finishes and its result clears; the check is a Redis transaction.
quote:
It guarantees
that a job with a particular ID cannot be enqueued again until its execution has finished and its result has cleared.
notes: Also: 'The check of ``job_id`` uniqueness in the queue is performed using a redis transaction so you can be certain jobs with the same id won't be enqueued twice (or overwritten) even if they're enqueued at exactly the same time.'

claim: Dramatiq only acks a message after processing finishes (late ack, at-least-once), and this cannot be changed.
quote:
Celery acks tasks as soon as they’re pulled by a worker by
       default.  This is easy to change, but a bad default.  Dramatiq
       doesn’t let you change this: tasks are only ever acked when
       they’re done processing.
notes: Footnote in the Motivation page comparing to Celery. 'At least once' is our label; the docs here do not use that phrase.

claim: Dramatiq Retries middleware retries with exponential backoff: max_retries 20, min backoff 15 s, max backoff 7 days.
quote: max_retries: int = 20,
notes: Docstring in same file: 'Middleware that automatically retries failed tasks with exponential backoff.' and 'min_backoff(int): ... Defaults to 15 seconds.' 'max_backoff(int): ... Defaults to 7 days.' Fetched from master; v2.2.1 is the latest tag, verify line numbers if pinning.

claim: Dramatiq moves messages past their retry or age limits to a dead letter queue, kept 7 days then dropped.
quote:
Once a message has exceeded its retry or age limits, it gets moved to
the dead letter queue where it's kept for up to 7 days and then
automatically dropped from the message broker.
notes: Guide also: 'Dramatiq will keep retrying the message with longer and longer delays in between runs until we fix our code or for up to about 30 days from when it was first enqueued.'

claim: Durable execution: a workflow keeps its state and progress through failures, crashes and outages.
quote: Durable Execution in the context of Temporal refers to the ability of a Workflow Execution to maintain its state and progress even in the face of failures, crashes, or server outages.
notes: Extracted via WebFetch summariser; re-check wording on the live page before quoting on the page.

claim: Temporal workflow code must be deterministic: same API calls in the same order for the same input.
quote: Generally speaking, this means you must take care to ensure that any time your Workflow code is executed it makes the same Workflow API calls in the same sequence, given the same input.
notes: Extracted via WebFetch summariser.

claim: On replay, commands emitted by workflow code are matched against the stored Event History to rebuild state.
quote: When the Workflow's code replays, the Commands that are emitted are compared with the existing Event History. If a corresponding Event already exists within the Event History that matches that command, then the Execution progresses.
notes: Extracted via WebFetch summariser.

claim: Temporal activities may be retried and run more than once, so they should be idempotent.
quote: Temporal recommends that Activities be idempotent.
notes: Next sentence: 'Because Activities may be retried, these functions may be executed more than once.' Also: 'A non-idempotent Activity could adversely affect the state of the system.'

claim: Default Activity retry policy: 1 s initial interval, backoff 2.0, max interval 100x initial, unlimited attempts.
quote:
Initial Interval     = 1 second
Backoff Coefficient  = 2.0
Maximum Interval     = 100 × Initial Interval
Maximum Attempts     = ∞
notes: Same page: 'Temporal's default behavior is to automatically retry an Activity that fails'. Workflows themselves are not retried by default.

claim: Temporal and OpenAI released a Durable Execution integration for the OpenAI Agents SDK in public preview, July 2025.
quote: OpenAI and Temporal have teamed up to add Durable Execution to agents built using OpenAI's Agents SDK, and today we released the new integration in Public Preview.

claim: OpenAI uses Temporal; its VP of Infrastructure says OpenAI built a durable orchestration framework powered by Temporal.
quote: This is one of the main reasons why we invested in building a durable orchestration framework powered by Temporal at OpenAI.
notes: Quote attributed to Venkat Venkataramani, OpenAI VP of Infrastructure, inside a Temporal (vendor) funding post. Same post: 'OpenAI's use of Temporal has grown 60-fold in under a year.' Vendor source, not OpenAI's own site.

claim: OpenAI Codex runs on Temporal.
notes: unconfirmed: no primary source found naming Codex. Checked the Agents SDK announcement, temporal.io home page and the 2026 Series E post; none mention Codex. Do not state this on the page.

claim: DBOS is a library that durably executes annotated code, with queues backed by Postgres.
quote: DBOS is a library for building reliable programs. Add a few annotations to your application to durably execute it and make it resilient to any failure.
notes: Same page: 'Lightweight, durable, distributed queues backed by Postgres'.

claim: Restate durable execution stores completed steps and resumes from there after failure.
quote: Code automatically stores completed steps and resumes from where it left off when recovering from failures.
notes: Extracted via WebFetch summariser.

claim: A Kubernetes CronJob creates a Job approximately once per schedule time; sometimes two or none, so Jobs should be idempotent.
quote:
A CronJob creates a Job object approximately once per execution time of its schedule.
The scheduling is approximate because there
are certain circumstances where two Jobs might be created, or no Job might be created.
Kubernetes tries to avoid those situations, but does not completely prevent them. Therefore,
the Jobs that you define should be _idempotent_.
notes: Verified from source https://github.com/kubernetes/website/blob/main/content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs.md (main branch, fetched 2026-10-04).

claim: concurrencyPolicy: Allow (default) runs overlapping Jobs, Forbid skips the new run, Replace replaces the running Job.
quote:
* `Allow` (default): The CronJob allows concurrently running Jobs
* `Forbid`: The CronJob does not allow concurrent runs; if it is time for a new Job run and the
  previous Job run hasn't finished yet, the CronJob skips the new Job run.
notes: Replace: 'If it is time for a new Job run and the previous Job run hasn't finished yet, the CronJob replaces the currently running Job run with a new Job run'. Also: 'Note that concurrency policy only applies to the Jobs created by the same CronJob.'

claim: startingDeadlineSeconds: if a Job misses its start time by more than this, that run is skipped.
quote:
The `.spec.startingDeadlineSeconds` field is optional.
This field defines a deadline (in whole seconds) for starting the Job, if that Job misses its scheduled time
for any reason.

After missing the deadline, the CronJob skips that instance of the Job (future occurrences are still scheduled).
notes: Also: if unset and more than 100 schedules are missed (e.g. controller down), the Job will not start.

claim: Airflow: treat tasks like database transactions; since Airflow retries, tasks must produce the same outcome on every re-run.
quote: Airflow can retry a task if it fails. Thus, the tasks should produce the same outcome on every re-run.
notes: Preceding: 'You should treat tasks in Airflow equivalent to transactions in a database. This implies that you should never produce incomplete results from your tasks.' Extracted via WebFetch summariser.

claim: Little's Law: average number in system L equals average arrival rate lambda times average time in system W.
quote:
Little’s Law says that the average number of items in a
queuing system, denoted L, equals the average arrival rate
of items to the system, λ, multiplied by the average waiting
time of an item in the system, W . Thus,
L = λW
notes: Text read from PDF copy at https://people.cs.umass.edu/~emery/classes/cmpsci691st/readings/OS/Littles-Law-50-Years-Later.pdf (publisher page returned 403). PDF font maps lambda to 'ã'; restored as λ.

claim: Precondition: classic proofs need the three averages to exist and converge over an infinite horizon (long-run, stable system); over a finite window it holds exactly if the system starts and ends empty.
quote:
Most sample path proofs of Little’s Law (Stidham 1974,
Whitt 1991, Wolff 2011) analyze queuing processes over
the entire time axis (0 ≤ t < ∞) and show that L = λW ,
subject to the existence and convergence of the three LL
parameters, and possibly other conditions.
notes: PDF glyphs restored (≤, ∞, λ). Section 2.1.2 heading: 'Proof of Little’s Law for a System Empty at 0 and T'. A growing backlog (arrival rate above service rate) never converges, so L = λW does not describe it.

claim: A queue-based system is bimodal: fast with no backlog, then once arrivals exceed processing, latency grows and recovery takes a long time.
quote: Putting it another way, a queue-based system has two modes of operation, or bimodal behavior. When there is no backlog in the queue, the system’s latency is low, and the system is in fast mode. But if a failure or unexpected load pattern causes the arrival rate to exceed the processing rate, it quickly flips into a more sinister operating mode. In this mode, the end-to-end latency grows higher and higher, and it can take a great deal of time to work through the backlog to return to the fast mode.
notes: Text verified from the Wayback Machine copy of the original URL https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/ (snapshot 20240124001614), which now 301-redirects to builder.aws.com; the builder.aws.com page is JS-rendered and could not be read directly. Author: David Yanacek.

claim: An hour-long outage needs double capacity for another hour to recover; async systems trade dropped requests for long recovery.
quote: Imagine a system that experiences an hour-long outage while processing messages. Regardless of the given rate and processing capacity, recovering from the outage requires double the system’s capacity for another hour after the recovery.
notes: Same article: 'Asynchronous services build up backlogs during outages, leading to long recovery times, unlike synchronous services, which drop requests during outages but have quicker recover times.' Text verified from the Wayback Machine copy of the original URL https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/ (snapshot 20240124001614), which now 301-redirects to builder.aws.com; the builder.aws.com page is JS-rendered and could not be read directly. Author: David Yanacek.

claim: A 30-minute unthrottled spike at 10x consumer capacity takes 300 minutes to drain.
quote: But if the volume of queued messages was 10x the capacity that the consumer side was scaled to, this means it would take 300 minutes for the system to work through the backlog and recover. Even short load spikes can result in multi-hour recovery times, and therefore cause multi-hour outages.
notes: Text verified from the Wayback Machine copy of the original URL https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/ (snapshot 20240124001614), which now 301-redirects to builder.aws.com; the builder.aws.com page is JS-rendered and could not be read directly. Author: David Yanacek.

claim: Measure the age of messages in the queue (from the enqueue timestamp), not just producer latency.
quote: Therefore, we focus more on measuring the age of messages that are in the queue. This quickly catches cases where the systems are behind, or are frequently erroring out and causing retries.
notes: Text verified from the Wayback Machine copy of the original URL https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/ (snapshot 20240124001614), which now 301-redirects to builder.aws.com; the builder.aws.com page is JS-rendered and could not be read directly. Author: David Yanacek.

claim: Real-time systems use FIFO-ish queues but customers prefer LIFO-ish behaviour: fresh data first after a backlog.
quote: Real time systems often are implemented with FIFO-ish queues, but prefer LIFO-ish behavior.
notes: Next: 'We hear from our customers that when faced with a backlog, they prefer to see their fresh data processed immediately. Any data accumulated during an outage or surge can then be processed as capacity is available.' Text verified from the Wayback Machine copy of the original URL https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/ (snapshot 20240124001614), which now 301-redirects to builder.aws.com; the builder.aws.com page is JS-rendered and could not be read directly. Author: David Yanacek.

claim: AWS Lambda hashes each customer to a few of a fixed set of queues and enqueues into the shortest, isolating noisy customers (shuffle sharding).
quote: So rather than using one queue, AWS Lambda provisions a fixed number of queues, and hashes each customer to a small number of queues. Before enqueueing a message, it checks to see which of those targeted queues contains the fewest messages, and enqueues into that one. When one customer’s workload increases, it will drive a backlog in its mapped queues, but other workloads will automatically be routed away from those queues.
notes: Also covers per-customer queues: 'Instead of sharing one queue across all customers, in some systems we give each customer its own queue.' Text verified from the Wayback Machine copy of the original URL https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/ (snapshot 20240124001614), which now 301-redirects to builder.aws.com; the builder.aws.com page is JS-rendered and could not be read directly. Author: David Yanacek.

claim: Sideline old messages to a backlog queue so fresh messages are served first, approximating LIFO.
quote: When we dequeue a message, we can check how old it is. Rather than just logging the age, we can use the information to decide whether to move the message into a backlog queue that we work through only after we’re caught up on the live queue.
notes: Ends: 'This is one way to approximate LIFO ordering.' Text verified from the Wayback Machine copy of the original URL https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/ (snapshot 20240124001614), which now 301-redirects to builder.aws.com; the builder.aws.com page is JS-rendered and could not be read directly. Author: David Yanacek.

claim: Some systems can drop old messages (TTL), e.g. when a periodic full sync (anti-entropy sweeper) will cover them.
quote: Some systems can tolerate very old messages being dropped. For example, some systems process deltas to systems quickly, but also do full synchronization periodically. We often call these periodic synchronization systems anti-entropy sweepers. In these cases, instead of sidelining old queued up traffic, we can cheaply drop it if it came in before the most recent sweep.
notes: Section heading 'Dropping old messages (message time-to-live)'. Text verified from the Wayback Machine copy of the original URL https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/ (snapshot 20240124001614), which now 301-redirects to builder.aws.com; the builder.aws.com page is JS-rendered and could not be read directly. claim: Little's Law applied: 100 messages/s at 100 ms uses 10 threads; if latency jumps to 10 s, 1,000 threads.
quote: For example, if a server was processing 100 messages / sec at 100 ms average, it would consume 10 threads on average. If the latency suddenly spiked to 10 seconds, it would suddenly use 1,000 threads (on average, so it could be more in practice), which could easily exhaust a thread pool.
notes: Text verified from the Wayback Machine copy of the original URL https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/ (snapshot 20240124001614), which now 301-redirects to builder.aws.com; the builder.aws.com page is JS-rendered and could not be read directly.
